Despite its success, selecting the optimal GCN architecture remains a complex and time-consuming task, particularly due to the lack of comprehensive analysis on its core components, including the convolution operation and network depth. In this research, we investigate these aspects by comparing different methods and assessing their impact on point cloud-based tasks. Our findings reveal that the graph Laplacian is the most effective convolution method for graph-based neural networks and that an over-parameterized network does not yield improved performance. Furthermore, we introduce the GCN-3, an optimized GCN architecture featuring three linearly stacked layers, which exhibits superior empirical inductive performance compared to existing models.

Recent advancements in neural-based code detection have significantly improved the ability to identify malicious code, but research has shown that traditional, obfuscation-based techniques are insufficient to compromise its efficacy. This paper aims to explore the potential for developing code-assisted attacks that can bypass neural-based code detection systems, focusing on Dynamic Host-based Description (DHD) as a method to circumnavigate these systems, and subsequently, on creating Trojan programs that can evade them without employing any obfuscation techniques. Our findings demonstrate that such Hostless Trojans, which are generated using DHD, can evade neural-based code detection systems with a remarkable success rate of over 90%. Additionally, these Trojans are capable of executing complex operations, including interacting with various system components and manipulating files, while maintaining a high level of similarity to benign code, with a difference of less than 10% in terms of cosine distance. Our research also provides a framework for generating Hostless Trojans, along with a set of benchmarks to evaluate their effectiveness and a series of experiments to validate their capabilities.

We introduce an upgrade to the Magellan IMACS integral field integral camera, a significant component in astronomical observations. The upgrade involves integrating the ROSIE spectrograph, a highly advanced device with low dispersion and high resolution capabilities. By incorporating this upgrade, the imaging capabilities of IMACS will expand, allowing for observations across the UV to near-infrared spectrum with high-resolution settings. The expanded field of view will also accommodate smaller detectors, maximizing observational efficiency.

This paper discusses recent research on the fusion of carbon-12 with carbon-12 at low energies. We highlight key findings from our calculations and how they relate to experimental data. We also explore the potential of applying the Trojan horse method to studying this nuclear reaction.

The study focuses on the composition of exoplanet cores from a subset of stars that exhibit both terrestrial-type planets and detailed atmospheric layers of larger planets. A specific sample of 11 stars, which host planets resembling the Earth, was analyzed for their chemical composition. Chemical elements were measured using high-resolution spectroscopy, and the analysis revealed that most of these stars have metal abundances exceeding that of the sun. Furthermore, the study found that the metal content of these stars correlates with the mass of the accompanying giant planets. Utilizing existing models of planetary core formation, the research predicts that super-Earths formed from this star population would have higher core metal contents compared to those similar to the Earth.

Our innovative approach to indoor wireless localization leverages enhanced channel state information (CSI) obtained from commercial WiFi devices, which has been significantly impacted by indoor obstacles. To address this challenge, we develop a deep learning model that utilizes a combination of a convolutional neural network and an attention mechanism to extract relevant features from the WiFi signal. By utilizing real-world data collected in an office space, which includes precise location labels, we demonstrate that our method achieves high accuracy in determining user locations without the need for labeled data training. Furthermore, by training our model on a single data point, we are able to achieve impressive localization performance across different areas of the office space.

This paper proposes an innovative framework for the semantic interpretation of basic modal logic by redefining its constructs within topological categories that incorporate closed subsets and relations, in place of the traditional approach based on Kripke structures. In this new method, box and diamond operators are interpreted as universal and existential quantifiers respectively, thereby unifying modal and first-order logic semantics. This proposed framework will be extended in Part II to include the semantic analysis of first-order logic.

A bipartite graph's edges can be broken down into a set of cycles and another path. For bipartite graphs with specific properties, it has been proven that their edges can be broken down into a set of cycles. It has been proven that the 6-connected version of this property holds for certain graphs, but it has been found that a certain robust version of this property does not hold in the smallest connection version.

We investigate functions defined on the vertices of an n-dimensional hypercube, utilizing properties of the Hamming distance and assigning values from a set of (n+1) possible colors to each vertex based on the number of 1s in its binary representation. Let H_n represent this specific function, and we examine its eigenfunctions within the context of the Hamming graph, particularly its positive and negative first eigenvalues, denoted λ_1^+ and λ_1^- respectively. Our research focuses on the support sizes of functions bounded within these eigenvalue ranges, and we demonstrate the minimality of the support sizes for certain subsets within (n+1)λ_1^+ and -(n+1)λ_1^- intervals, including variations of H_n and functions with support sizes less than (n+1)λ_1^+ or -(n+1)λ_1^- in absolute value. Our proof leverages the semigroup property of the Hamming graph's adjacency matrix, and we also explore the implications of our findings in relation to the uncertainty principle in signal processing on graphs.

COPASI is a widely-used software tool for analyzing complex biological systems through mathematical modeling, although its user interface has been criticized for being unapproachable for many users. To address this issue, our team developed ShinyCOPASI, an application that enables users to interact with and run COPASI models via a web-based interface. Users can input, execute, and view results of simulations without needing additional software installation. To further enhance usability, we also created an API that allows users to control ShinyCOPASI using the COPASI Application Programming Interface.

This paper offers a comprehensive overview of current methodologies and evaluations used to measure ambiguity in artificial intelligence models. By defining and categorifying uncertainty types, we clarify the distinctions between them and review various evaluation protocols. Additionally, we propose and define standards for machine learning evaluations, emphasizing the need for clear benchmarks and metrics. Ultimately, this document serves as a reference for researchers and practitioners to choose evaluation methods that best suit their models and datasets.

We investigate a specific subalgebra of bounded operators on a complex vector space associated with a compact quantum group, defined by a category, and examine its properties including simplicity under certain conditions. Additionally, we investigate whether this algebra is a factor, establishing criteria for this property and providing concrete examples of algebras that do and do not satisfy the factor property.

This paper introduces a modified Strategy Iteration strategy that leverages the inexact GMRES method for solving large sparse linear systems in extensive Markov decision processes. A matrix with specific properties related to its nonnegative entries and a given vector with a positive sum is considered. By analyzing SI's convergence behavior under these properties, a new variant of inexact GMRES tailored for SI is proposed. Experimental results using examples from a board game demonstrate that this tailored variant outperforms conventional variations.

In a weighted directed graph G with n vertices and edges e, let I_G be the edge ideal generated by the weights of the edges. We will demonstrate that the regularity of I_G is less than or equal to the sum of the ranks of its edges minus one, extending a known result for undirected graphs. We will also identify conditions under which this equality holds, providing a potential counterexample to show these constraints are the tightest possible. Furthermore, we will establish a connection between the working edges of G and the minimal symbolic powers of I_G.

Computer-based simulations allow us to create artificial data according to specified parameters, which can then be used to generate corresponding synthetic data sets. By applying a certain criterion to these collections, we can evaluate a specific parameter of interest. This process is known as an artificial data-driven assessment and has become a valuable tool for understanding complex systems, such as in the fields of education, where it helps researchers gain insights without making inferences about real-world phenomena. Advances in computational power have made it possible to create large numbers of such data sets in a short amount of time, which has led to the development of new methods for understanding multiple data series, such as those that incorporate clustering and other analytical techniques.

A key challenge in deploying machine learning models in real-world settings is the issue of out-of-distribution data, which can cause them to malfunction. To overcome this limitation, several methods have been developed to train models that can learn from multiple data sources and adapt to variations in their distributions. We introduce the concept of regional queries, which involves each participant sending data to a central server along with an indication of the region it belongs to, allowing the server to update models for each region and then distribute them accordingly. This approach has the advantage of reducing the communication burden on participants and ensuring that each participant receives models tailored to their specific data distribution. We investigate the conditions under which regional queries can lead to improved model performance and demonstrate that, in some cases, they enable the participants to use a single model without the need for model averaging, which can be beneficial for privacy and performance.

Measurements of jet fragmentation in PbPb collisions, specifically those involving an isolated high-transverse-momentum photon, have been conducted at the LHC. By analyzing the distribution of charged-particle multiplicity within cones centered on the jet axis, the fragmentation pattern of the jet can be determined. This analysis, which accounts for the effects of an isolated photon on the fragmentation pattern, reveals that jets originating from photon-pair events exhibit a broader charged-particle distribution compared to those from proton-proton collisions. Notably, this phenomenon is more pronounced in PbPb collisions than in proton-proton collisions, suggesting a disruption in the fragmentation pattern due to the presence of the photon.

Recent research has provided novel findings on F-type series, enabling proof of F-type series identities, which possess significant connections to the values of colored multiple zeta expressions. This current study builds upon previous work, specifically continuing the investigation into F-type series and fast evaluations of modulated F-type series. Key accomplishments in this area include the derivation of non-hypergeometric Apéry-type series with recursive relationships, summation terms that can be expressed in modulated F-type series form, and series involving central binomial coefficients that adhere to the stuffle algebra of colored multiple zeta expressions. These accomplishments are achieved by constructing generating functions and applying projective symmetry principles.

A thorough investigation of the enigmatic brown dwarf, WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, also known as "The Mishap," is presented. This unique object, characterized by its extremely low temperature, is notable for its unusual spectral features. Spectral analysis reveals that its effective temperature is approximately 450-500 K, placing it at the lower end of the L spectral type. Notably, its spectral energy distribution is significantly distorted by interstellar dust, which affects the accuracy of its spectral classification. By combining various observational data, including photometry and spectroscopy, researchers have determined that this brown dwarf's spectral features are best explained by a combination of thermal emission and scattered light. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the physical properties of "The Mishap," shedding light on the complex nature of this unique celestial object.

Our analysis involves the creation of various particles such as pions, kaons, protons, antiprotons, and phi mesons in antiproton lead–gold collisions at a specific energy level of 5.44 TeV per nucleon pair. This is based on data collected by the CMS detector at the LHC and corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 0.3 nb^-1. The findings are further analyzed in comparison to data from similar processes and theoretical models predicting the behavior of these particles under certain conditions.

We've developed novel, efficient algorithms for interpolating and progressing parton distribution functions (PDFs) with high precision, resolving an ongoing issue in PDF analysis. Our solutions employ Almgren-Symes curves, which we've found to be more effective than traditional solutions to L^{\infty} functional differential equations. By utilizing these curves, computational resources are significantly reduced, as demonstrated in our tests at next-to-leading order using CT14 PDFs. Our methods are universally applicable and can be integrated with any PDF model or evolution framework, addressing a longstanding challenge in PDF analysis.

In-situ construction on other celestial bodies like the Moon and Mars could be facilitated by using regolith with local heating techniques such as microwave, solar, and Joule heating. By applying heat to regolith while in a compacted state, new bonds can form between the grains, a process known as in-situ sintering. This study aims to examine the effects of sintering heat on the microstructure and mechanical properties of compacted Martian and lunar regolith samples. Using scanning electron microscopy and micro-computed tomography, the samples were analyzed to understand their microstructure changes, and their mechanical properties were evaluated through compression tests. The results indicate that the optimal sintering temperature for improved mechanical properties lies between 400 and 600°C for both types of samples, and the mechanical properties of the samples increase with higher heat input and compaction density.

The development of droplets from an inclined liquid film on a fiber is examined,
focusing on the transition between two distinct regimes: those governed by capillary forces
and those influenced by viscous effects.  When the film breaks, a droplet forms and continues
to grow as it moves down the fiber, with its velocity determined by capillary forces in the first regime
and viscous effects in the second.  This process is consistent across both regimes, providing a unified
understanding of droplet formation and movement.

We have developed a new star formation rate indicator based on the ratio of Pa$\alpha$ to Brackett-$\gamma$ emission, which offers a reliable tool for measuring star formation rates in the mid-infrared range. This marker is particularly effective for young star clusters and OB associations, where other indicators like H$\alpha$ are compromised by dust. By comparing star formation rates derived from various tracers, we have found that Pa$\gamma$ is a more accurate representation of intrinsic H$\alpha$ than Brackett-$\gamma$ alone. This new star formation rate indicator has been validated through the analysis of 11 regions in the Carina Nebula Complex, where we have found that it is not affected by the presence of dust or ionizing photons. Furthermore, we have found that the ratio of Pa$\gamma$ to H$\alpha$ is a reliable indicator of ionization by massive stars, which can be used to study the physical properties of star-forming regions.

This paper delves into the symmetries of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$'s regional algebras, specifically $Q_N(\lambda)$, and their connections to the centralizer of Hecke algebra actions within the weight spaces of irreducible Verma modules, a concept explored in Part II of [KMM+21]. It is demonstrated that Hecke algebra actions commute with those of $Q_N(\lambda)$, leading to the conclusion that the centralizer is generated by the union of these two algebraic entities.

In 1956, the International Congress on Physical Chemistry in London marked a turning point for diffusion research, diffraction, and light scattering when Rayleigh's universal diffusion theory was introduced. This groundbreaking work laid the foundation for determining molecular weights, molecular dimensions, and even the friction coefficients and scattering of macromolecules, all based on the analysis of scattering patterns. This book delves into modern research in this field, presenting new theoretical concepts and experimental methods that build upon the foundation of Rayleigh's work.

A key component of a Human Computer Interface (HCI) is recognizing mathematical expressions, particularly when expressed through a graphics tablet equipped with sensors. Although graphics tablets excel at capturing spatial information like direction and movement, the specific nuances of writing mathematical expressions are often not fully explored. In this research, we aim to demonstrate the value of tracking hand movements while writing mathematical expressions and develop a classification system incorporating these motions. By analyzing sensor data from graphics tablets, we found distinct patterns for individual mathematical symbols and overall expressions, revealing that movement characteristics can effectively differentiate between similar symbols and expressions. Our results indicate that a classification model utilizing motion data achieves exceptional performance, with an accuracy of 98.5% on training data and 97.8% on test data.

To generate synthetic speech durations, traditional methods rely on statistical models, but a non-statistical approach can significantly reduce the required training data. A median-based method, widely used in clinical settings, calculates a central value that divides a set of data into two equal halves. This study evaluates the effectiveness of the median-driven non-statistical method for calculating synthetic speech durations. A total of 120 speakers were analyzed, with 60 using real data and 60 using artificially created data. The results showed that real data from speakers with hearing aids did not align with the median, whereas artificially created data from normal hearing speakers matched the median, indicating a potential benefit of the non-statistical method for speakers using hearing aids.

Conservation efforts require accurate assessment of species' habitats. However, collecting precise data can be challenging, leading to inaccuracies in modeling species' distributions. Ignoring data inaccuracies can result in flawed conclusions, hindering informed decision-making. This study introduces spHabitat, an R package that enables the application of spatial presence models to integrate covariates, observation uncertainty, and spatial trends in species' habitat modeling. These models can be utilized for single-species analysis, multi-species assessments, or integrated evaluations of species communities. The package supports model comparison and inference through the use of widely accessible R tools, facilitating ease of use for ecologists.

Skin lesions that indicate skin cancer are a significant global health issue, with many people struggling to recognize early signs of the disease. While dermatologists can accurately diagnose malignant lesions, they often experience eye strain and fatigue due to the repetitive nature of their work. The development of a dermoscopy image analysis tool has shown promise in assisting dermatologists, but many existing tools lack the ability to handle complex decision-making processes, learn from ongoing changes, and provide explanations for their diagnoses. This research introduces a new approach to create a collaborative diagnostic tool that leverages profound learning to analyze skin lesion images and diagnose them accurately. The approach employs a hybrid model that combines the strengths of ensemble learning and stacked generalization, with multiple specialized classifiers that use different methods to analyze lesion features and provide a range of diagnostic possibilities. The approach also uses a meta-learner to synthesize the opinions of these classifiers and provide a final diagnosis, with the ability to learn from the interaction between human experts and the system. The approach has been tested on a large dataset of skin lesion images and has shown promising results, with the ability to diagnose lesions accurately and within a short period of time. The research demonstrates the potential of profound learning to revolutionize the way skin lesions are diagnosed, with the skincare initiative providing a framework for the development of similar systems in other areas of medical diagnosis.

A neural network approach is proposed to analyze Type Ia supernovae data, and it is argued that utilizing recurrent neural networks for classifying supernovae is beneficial due to the sequential nature of the data. A specific implementation of a stochastic autoencoder is developed for this purpose, and it is successfully applied to the CNN-SNe Ia dataset. The results indicate that our model effectively identifies SN Ia events and accurately classifies them based on their peak magnitude, and it is further demonstrated that the CNN-SNe Ia dataset contains non-linear events. In comparison with other models, our approach exhibits improved performance in both reconstructing and classifying the data.

We have obtained high-resolution near-infrared integral field spectroscopy of a highly magnified star-forming galaxy at z=2.09, revealing a detailed spatial distribution of gas and dust across the galaxy. The data show that gas and dust are dynamically connected, moving in the same direction but with different velocities, which suggests that outflows are driven by radiation pressure from newly formed stars. This connection is further supported by the presence of nitrogen-rich gas and the observed spatial distribution of elements within the galaxy. The findings indicate that the outflows are not yet fully developed and have not yet affected the outer regions of the galaxy. The results have significant implications for understanding the growth of galaxies and the growth of black holes during the galaxy formation process.

The growth dynamics of turbulent plumes are heavily influenced by the injection of particles, which in turn affects the incorporation rate of ambient fluid into the plume. Our research focuses on how particle-filled plumes behave in the early stages, where particle effects are significant. Using a combination of direct numerical simulations and theoretical models, we studied the incorporation rate of particles in both clean and particle-laden plumes. Our results show that when particles are present, the incorporation rate is initially unaffected, but later decreases due to drag forces and changes in the plume's internal velocity structure. Our findings are applicable to a range of plume types and provide valuable insights into the behavior of particle-laden flows.

Understanding the spread of epidemics in complex networks is crucial for predicting and controlling outbreaks. Traditional models that analyze epidemics on simple networks have limitations, particularly when dealing with higher-order interactions. Researchers have developed a new framework based on higher-order structures, allowing for more accurate modeling of epidemic thresholds in various types of networks. By considering hyperedges as higher-order interactions, researchers have derived a general condition for epidemic thresholds that applies to a wide range of network types. This new framework provides insights into how the network's structure affects the spread of epidemics, allowing for more informed decision-making in public health policy.

In two-dimensional materials, low-dimensional magnetism exhibits unique characteristics. Researchers have investigated the effects of reduced dimensionality on ferromagnetic chromium iodide (CrI3) bilayers, revealing a complex interplay between intrinsic order and external factors such as lattice distortions and interlayer interactions. A theoretical model incorporating the effects of lattice distortions and Rashba interactions has been developed, revealing that this combination can induce a canting of the ferromagnetic Cr spins towards their natural orientation along the a-axis, rather than their original orientation along the vertical axis. A comparison with experimental observations has confirmed the validity of this theoretical model, highlighting the importance of Rashba interactions in controlling the canting angle of the ferromagnetic Cr spins.

The majority of solar-like stars exhibit magnetic cycles similar to the Sun's, yet our understanding of the rotation patterns in these stars remains limited.  Recent research indicates that many stars rotate in a way that resembles the Sun's rotation, with significant differences in rotation rates between their equatorial and polar regions.  This study investigates how potential solar-like rotation patterns affect magnetic cycle dynamics through numerical simulations.  By altering the differential rotation strength and angular momentum transport mechanisms, the researchers found that cycles with the correct polarity reversal still emerge, but their characteristics change significantly.  Stronger differential rotation leads to a decline in the overall magnetic field intensity and delays cycle occurrence, while increased turbulent diffusivity causes cycle cessation.  The study's outcomes highlight the critical role of solar-like rotation patterns in determining magnetic cycle behavior and suggest that stars with similar rotation patterns may experience distinct cycle dynamics compared to those with uniform rotation distributions.

Deep learning models have achieved significant advancements in tasks such as classification and regression through the utilization of deep neural networks. However, these models have encountered limitations in addressing challenges related to multiple input data types, complex output formats, and complex input-output mappings. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a generalized k-fan multimodal deep framework that can handle multiple types of modalities and various problem domains. The framework is built on the foundation of multimodal deep learning and can be extended to handle complex mappings by incorporating auxiliary outputs. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed framework is universal, while empirical evaluations on multiple datasets show its efficacy in achieving state-of-the-art performance.

The increasing complexity of multithreaded code poses a significant challenge in detecting subtle concurrency errors, such as data races, which can lead to system instability and unpredictable behavior. The number of possible thread interleavings that need to be analyzed grows exponentially with system size, making full exploration impractical for systems with a large number of threads. To address this issue, researchers have developed model verification techniques that can efficiently identify relevant interleavings and verify system correctness. One such approach is Delay-Based Partial-Order Reduction (DPOR), which has been shown to be effective in detecting concurrency errors and has been integrated into modern multithreading debuggers and model verifiers. The McMini model verifier, based on DPOR, has been designed to be highly configurable and supports multiple types of concurrency checks, including total order, DPOR, and in-order checks. The tool has been shown to outperform other state-of-the-art model verifiers in terms of detection capabilities and has been used to detect a wide range of concurrency errors in multiple test suites.

The effectiveness of limiting WhatsApp message forwarding in countering misinformation spread is investigated. The study finds that while reducing allowed forwards per number can decrease overall share volume, the impact diminishes quickly as the reduction in allowed forwards per number shifts from one to zero. The research also shows that this policy can inadvertently create uneven sharing patterns, with some users forwarding more than others, and that the impact of the policy is more pronounced for smaller networks, particularly in countering misinformation spread.

We derive estimates for the distribution of allele frequencies for a rare allele in a large population, given that it originated from a single individual, and we also examine how this spectrum might be altered in situations where the population experiences significant growth.

This paper presents an innovative attentive activation mechanism designed to boost the efficiency of spoofing detection systems. The proposed method incorporates a dual-module structure, consisting of an activation module and a counteraction module, which are strategically integrated into an end-to-end spoofing counteraction system. The attentive activation mechanism is uniquely positioned to analyze and differentiate between genuine and spoofed audio based on its prior understanding of the distinction. The module's ability to make accurate predictions enables it to provide valuable insights to the end-to-end system, ultimately enhancing its performance. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed mechanism in achieving superior spoofing detection performance compared to existing methods.

In supersymmetric models, we investigate the constraints on inflationary scenarios, assuming that supersymmetry is broken through the mechanism of inflation within a supergravity framework. By analyzing the most supersymmetric and efficient models, we identify the limitations on inflationary parameters, finding that the inflationary potential closely resembles the Starobinsky model.

The detection of photon pairs is typically grouped based on the detection time of individual photons, an approach used to identify signal photons from spontaneous four-wave mixing, which is matched with a reference time frame, often established by a pump laser detection event. However, analysis of a large number of detection sequences reveals that only a fraction of these sequences contribute effectively to the elimination of random noise, or "background," suggesting that the conventional matching method inadequately utilizes available data. By optimizing the algorithm to maximize the subtraction of background correlations, we found that the contribution of random sequences can be nearly eliminated with just a fraction of the detection sequences used in traditional methods, thus significantly enhancing the measurement of signal photon intensities.

Our research focuses on near-field terahertz spectroscopy of superconducting qubits housed in coplanar microwave resonators. We utilize a terahertz-emitting tip to both stimulate and detect terahertz fields, with emitted radiation being efficiently captured and characterized via reflected signals. By measuring the phase and amplitude of these signals, we are able to map out standing terahertz waves resulting from superconducting coherence. Additionally, we are able to extract material properties such as thickness and complex permittivity from our experimental data.

We establish the minimum cardinality required for partitioning the real line into non-empty sets, where each collection consists of Borel measurable elements. Our findings generalize and refine earlier results obtained by various researchers including Sierpinski, Mycielski, Laver, and Shelah.

In light of the stagnation of traditional investment returns, there is a growing interest in exploring new approaches. To this end, we examine the impact of introducing alternative trading strategies on market returns through simulations. Our model incorporates virtual traders who execute trades based on either a pre-established set of rules or an adaptive process that allows them to discover new strategies. When these novel strategies are introduced, we find that they have the potential to elevate market returns, particularly in markets characterized by limited trading activity. Conversely, in more active markets, the introduction of novel strategies does not have a significant effect on returns.

Identifying the protocol being used in a network communication is a crucial step in network defense. This process is complicated by the rapid development of new protocols, which can make it difficult for automated systems to keep up. As a result, researchers have developed automated tools to assist in this identification process, but these tools are vulnerable to attacks that can deceive them and cause system failures. In this paper, we analyze the limitations of two open-source tools used for automated protocol identification, exposing flaws in their design that can be exploited by malicious actors.

We investigate the behavior of thermal gating in magnons within a system that includes a superconducting strip placed in close proximity to a magnetic strip. The presence of the superconducting strip leads to an accumulation of energy at the interface between the superconductor and the magnetic strip. This energy accumulation gives rise to a slight increase in the magnetic stripe's Curie temperature, $T_c$. The magnitude of the $T_c$ shift depends on the superconducting gap, $\Delta$, and is significantly larger in the case of $s$-wave superconductors compared to unconventional superconductors with node in the gap function. The observed $T_c$ shift is consistent with the energy accumulation at the interface and can be understood in terms of a heat bath provided by the superconducting near-field.

A notable obstacle in federated learning is the participation of new edge devices with unique categories, posing a challenge as their data and model information must be securely exchanged. Overcoming this challenge involves overcoming data privacy concerns in distributed settings. This research introduces ZSFL, an innovative approach enabling the training and inference of a deep learning model on audio classification with the participation of new devices having unseen categories without requiring any prior data sharing. ZSFL utilizes a shared matrix factorization matrix to represent device-specific audio data and shared labels, facilitating secure data transmission. ZSFL's performance is evaluated on UrbanSound8K, a widely-used audio dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in training a deep learning model with participating new devices containing unseen categories, surpassing the performance of baseline methods.

Experimental verification of the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger effect in quantum physics has been accomplished in multiple experiments involving numerous particles or parties. However, the current evaluation methods are limited to lower-dimensional systems due to an exponential increase in complexity with dimensionality. A new method is proposed to handle these challenges by first determining the maximum number of linear inequalities that can be satisfied with a certain degree of accuracy, and then using these results to calculate the quantum bounds for general GHZ states involving a specific amount of entanglement. This method is demonstrated in an experiment where it is applied to a system of 12 entangled photons, and the experiment confirms the maximum number of violated inequalities, and the theoretical quantum bound is closely matched.

In a wireless communication system with multiple users and a smart reflecting surface, the complex multiplication of channel vectors makes direct full-dimensional channel estimation impractical due to excessive pilot overhead. A proposed method estimates the channel in two steps: first, it determines the optimal pilot sequence and calculates the channel from the direct link between the base station and the array, then calculates the user-specific reflected channel based on the direct link and user location, significantly reducing the required information exchange and pilot overhead. The effectiveness of this scheme is validated through numerical results.

This research investigates the relationship between regional U.S. news consumption, local COVID-19 pandemic coverage, and changes in news audience demographics. We utilize data from Nielsen, GDELT, and local health departments to understand news engagement patterns and the correlation between news consumption and pandemic response. Our results show that local news consumption is linked to lower COVID-19 mortality rates, suggesting that effective communication of local pandemic information may play a crucial role in public health measures adherence.

This research investigates the capabilities of neural networks in learning basic counting principles from the ground up, without prior instruction, by developing and refining a specialized model designed to master a complex task - mapping the progression of counting numbers. The study reveals that, although the neural network is successful in mastering the task, its performance is significantly hindered when the task size exceeds a certain threshold - the point at which the model's internal structure can no longer efficiently represent the task's inherent mathematical properties. The research proposes an improved model, incorporating enhanced memory capabilities, that can achieve a level of accuracy comparable to its smaller counterpart, thereby overcoming the limitations of the original model's size and demonstrating the potential for neural networks to be used in studying the development of fundamental cognitive skills in humans.

Bloom filters excel at identifying non-existent items but fall short on exact matches. A variant called the Bloom cactus filter addresses this limitation, yet it comes with increased memory requirements. In contrast, the Bloom filter and its successor, the Cuckoo filter, strike a balance between precision and efficiency by utilizing slightly more memory for identifying existing items. Our Bloom xor filter achieves even better results by utilizing less memory for identifying existing items. This innovative approach combines a Bloom filter with parity checks for each bit, enabling the detection of existing items even if some elements are missing. Our modified structure supports multiple deletion operations and offers faster and more accurate identification of existing items than the Bloom cactus filter. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of the Bloom xor filter in terms of time and space complexity.

The broader field of monomials in multiple variables contains interesting connections between convex geometry and holomorphic functions, which can be measured by a association function related to order types of subsets in $\mathbb{N}^{d}$. A related concept involves Gromov's work on volumes of symplectic spaces, which ties in with this connection function.

In the stock trading domain, accurately forecasting market trends is a critical challenge. This paper presents an innovative approach to trend prediction by focusing on sequential cost functions derived from historical transaction data, specifically the time series of cost functions associated with each transaction. This time series data, consisting of execution costs, shared speeds, and corresponding sale volumes, provides valuable insights into market dynamics. By analyzing these costs, our model can effectively capture and represent market trends, outperforming existing methods in multiple market environments.

The surge in data sharing has led to significant concerns regarding user privacy, leading researchers to turn to federated learning as a viable solution. Privacy-preserving federated learning methods, such as differential privacy and secure multi-party computation, have been developed to protect user information, but they come with drawbacks in terms of communication efficiency and computational costs. In contrast, our novel framework combines the strengths of federated learning and secure multi-party computation to address these challenges, specifically designed to protect data during differential computing. The framework, named FLVoogd, leverages secret sharing and homomorphic encryption to prevent data manipulation and ensure user privacy, while also allowing for the verification of computations and the detection of malicious behaviors. The results demonstrate that FLVoogd outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, communication efficiency, and resilience, even in the presence of malicious users.

This study presents a novel Sim2Real technique for bridging the gap between simulated and real-world data, specifically for 2D navigation tasks in aerial images. Traditional Sim2Real methods often rely on data augmentation or model retraining, which can be ineffective for navigation tasks due to the complex relationships between image features and navigation actions. Our approach leverages image segmentation masks from simulated data to calculate feature importance for action prediction, and uses this information to create corresponding action layers in real-world data. By fine-tuning a pre-trained action prediction model on the filtered real-world data, we can significantly improve its performance on navigation tasks. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in enhancing navigation accuracy.

The growing concern surrounding the creation and dissemination of manipulated media has led to the need for advanced techniques in creating and detecting manipulated content. Building on previous research, this study presents two innovative frameworks: one for creating highly realistic manipulations of unrestricted content and another for identifying the artificial manipulations. The creation framework utilizes a generative model to produce authentic video clips, which are then combined with specific actions, generated by the identification model, to produce manipulated content. The resulting manipulations are highly realistic and can be accurately detected by the identification model. In a series of experiments, the proposed creation framework outperformed existing methods in producing realistic manipulations, achieving scores of 0.76 on the AVCLiAR dataset and 0.69 on the Deepfake-Creation dataset. Additionally, the identification model achieved scores of 0.55 and 0.51, respectively, on the same datasets, demonstrating its accuracy in detecting manipulations.

The discovery of sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets has been accelerating, but the composition of these planets remains largely unknown. Theoretical models suggest that many of these planets could be composed of large amounts of water, but the extent of this is uncertain. The presence of water in these planets could lead to concealed oceans, but the composition of their atmospheres could also be influenced by other factors, such as hydrogen and helium. The composition of these planets could be modeled using a two-layer system, where the upper layer is composed of gas and the lower layer is composed of liquid water. The composition of these planets could be further constrained by the presence of clouds and hazes, which could obscure the composition of their atmospheres. The composition of these planets could be further constrained by the presence of atmospheric features, such as sodium and potassium, which could be detected during transit observations.
